label: Claude Haiku 5.5
output:
# Toast at Four

I did my last night shift on Saturday. Nine at night to half seven in the morning, majors, the usual mix of chest pain that turned out to be anxiety and anxiety that turned out to be chest pain. I handed over, signed off the board, and walked out into a morning that was already bright, which felt like an unfair thing for the day to do.

From Monday I'm on days only. After fourteen years of nights I finally have the rota I asked for, and I am, to my surprise, not okay about it.

I've tried to write about this a few times since spring. Every draft turns into an obituary for a way of working, or a list of everything wrong with the place, and I don't want either. I want to be honest about what nights gave me and what they took. The rest can wait for another day.

The reasons are good ones. My knees have had enough of stairs at half four in the morning. My sleep has never recovered its shape, and I've stopped pretending it will. And the GP, who is sensible and has been patient with me for a while, finally said my blood pressure was not something to keep joking about. So this is the right decision. I know that. Knowing it doesn't seem to do much for the feeling.

I started nights in 2012 as an SHO, twenty-eight and very sure I'd be the one who could cope. Fourteen years is a lot of Decembers. It's a lot of 3am handovers and early-morning drives with the sun coming up the wrong way, and the kind of tiredness that doesn't leave so much as settle in and make itself at home.

The first winter, I cried in the car park at the Infirmary. I'd come off a run of shifts and was sitting in the car, unable to remember whether I'd given the second dose of something to someone. I went back in and checked. I had. I still remember the frost on the windscreen while I sat there with my hands in my lap, trying to make the thought stop going round. I think that was the first time I understood that nights would ask things of me that I'd have to learn to carry, not just survive.

People assume nights are about adrenaline. There's some of that. The department at 2am can feel like a film set with the lights turned up. But mostly, I'd say, nights are about staying kind at five in the morning when you're completely empty. Adrenaline wears off in an hour. Kindness has to be found again every time, from a smaller pot each time, and you find it because the person in front of you is frightened and it's your job to be the calm one. Most nights I managed. Some I didn't, and I won't pretend otherwise.

One winter, around three in the morning, I was looking after an older man who was frightened in the particular way people are when they don't know where they are. I sat with him for a while. At some point he took my hand, very firmly, and told me I had his daughter's hands. I didn't correct him, and I didn't need to. When I think about that night, it's usually the hand I think about.

Nights are where the department is most itself. There are fewer managers in the corridor, fewer emails, fewer people with opinions about the rota. What's left is the people actually doing the work, and an unvarnished honesty that only comes out late. You stop performing. Patients tell you the truth because it's late and they're tired of hiding it. Colleagues do too. The kindness is less about policy and more about who's still awake and still choosing to be decent when nobody is watching. I've loved that part more than I can easily say.

And nights took things. I missed both my nieces' naming ceremonies. I watched them on video from a staff room with a cold cup of tea, holding the phone at an angle so the screen wouldn't catch the strip lights. My sister, who is in Bangalore and has been doing most of the family-keeping from the other side of the world, never once complained. Not once. I don't think I've ever properly thanked her for that, so I'm putting it here. Thank you.

I've missed other things too. Weddings I wanted to be at, Christmas mornings, the ordinary Tuesdays that turn out to be the ones you remember. I've been tired in ways that made me short with people I love. I've been a worse friend than I wanted to be. Those costs are real, and I'd be lying if I said I'd have paid them without a second thought.

On Sunday morning I drove home down the London Road. The sun was coming up low and gold over the rooftops, and I had the radio on catch-up, the shipping forecast going through its sea areas in that calm, slightly hypnotic voice. Dogger, Fisher, German Bight. It was the most ordinary thing in the world, and I found myself getting teary at the lights by the junction. I realised I wouldn't see that particular light from this side of the job again. That's what I didn't expect. Not the shifts, not the handover, but the drive home.

Then there's the relief, which is the part I feel least able to talk about. I'm relieved, and it feels almost like abandonment, as if being glad to stop means I've let something down. I keep thinking about the colleagues still on nights, some of whom have done it longer than me, and I feel like a traitor for being glad to step off. I don't think I am. I think I've given what I could, my body and my family have been asking for something back, and I'm allowed to answer them.

So I'll end somewhere lighter, because that's true too.

Someone always makes toast in the staff room at four in the morning. Always. There's a toaster that is older than most of the junior doctors, and every night someone puts two slices in and waits. Nobody admits to starting it. I've asked. I've asked for fourteen years and never got a straight answer. It's the most reliable thing about nights, more reliable than the rota or the coffee machine. Someone decides, quietly, that everyone deserves a bit of warm bread at the worst hour, and then they make it without fuss and leave the crumbs for whoever comes next.

And Folasade. Folasade has been charge nurse on nights for twenty-two years, and she still beats me up the stairs. I've tried to keep up with her for years and never managed it. She has seen more nights than I have, more winters, more of the people who come through those doors at their worst, and she has never once stopped being kind to them or to the rest of us. If you want to know what nights are for, watch her at a bedside at five in the morning. You'll see it.

I don't yet know what I'll do with my body clock on Monday, or what mornings will feel like when they aren't the morning after a shift. But the toaster will still be there. Someone will still be making toast at four. And somewhere in that building there will be a woman still beating everyone up the stairs. That's enough to be going on with.

reasons: The piece says the doctor watched the naming ceremonies on video, rather than missing them, and adds that the older man was frightened and did not know where he was.
